newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian lead on Zaire bold but risky.
newsitem.headline: Canadian lead on Zaire bold but risky.

text.p: In seizing the lead in arranging a military aid mission to Zaire, Canada has taken a risky gamble to burnish an image tarnished by past missions to Africa.

Frustrated by international dithering on Zaire, Prime Minister Jean Chretien took the plunge last weekend by offering Canadian leadership of the mission. He called at least 18 national leaders since Saturday to rally support.

"Obviously the prime minister felt the urgency of the situation and wanted to move it forward," his spokeswoman Leslie Swartman said. "Canada is well-known for our peacekeeping. We have no colonial ties to the countries in the region and we're a bilingual country," she said.

If Canada succeeds in alleviating the hunger of a million refugees caught in fighting in eastern Zaire, and possibly helps restore peace, it will help erase the memory of unsuccessful or tragic missions to Somalia and Rwanda.

Besides failing to put an end to the strife in Somalia, Canada's peacekeeping record was sullied by the torturing and/or killing of Somalis in 1993 and a subsequent coverup that is still being investigated in Canada.
Canadian command of the U.N. mission in Rwanda -- dealing with the same ethnic mix of Tutsis and Hutus -- failed to prevent the slaughter of a million people there in 1994.

"(It is) incredibly risky ... unless they go in with a lot of clout and are prepared to kill a lot of people if they have to," said retired Brig. Gen. Jim Hanson, associate executive director of the Canadian Institute of Strategic Studies.

"Right now you've got potentially a three-way war and you put the U.N. troops in there and it turns it into a four-way war. How do you tell the bad guys from the good guys? You're going to be dealing with the Zairean army, ... the Tutsi rebels in Zaire, and then you're going to be dealing with the Hutu extremists in the refugee camps and that's not even talking about the official government of Rwanda and the official government of Burundi."
Hanson said in such circumstances everybody often gangs up on the peacekeepers and unless difficult political agreements were reached it might be difficult to leave.
Member of Parliament Bob Mills, foreign affairs spokesman for the opposition Reform Party, said clear questions needed to be asked lest Canada enter a "black hole."
"We have to have a withdrawal strategy before we go in," he told Reuters, referring to the extended missions in places like Bosnia and Haiti.

Swartman commented: "It's never a sure thing. There is certainly a risk." But she said Chretien, whose nephew Raymond Chretien is the U.N. troubleshooter trying to solve the crisis, felt strongly something had to be done.

One difference from the earlier trouble in Rwanda was that military planners were talking about a much larger force -- somewhere around 10,000 strong. Maj. Gen. Romeo Dallaire complained bitterly about the inadequacy of the 2,500 troops he had as commander of the U.N. force in Rwanda.
